questions.stem: Two observers dispute a claim; one has better instruments; how should the claim be judged?

options.text: The better-instrumented observer's claim carries more weight
Both are equally right regardless of instruments
The dispute means no conclusion is possible
The older observer is always correct

questions.explanation: Better instruments give more weight; equality ignores evidence quality.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A hypothesis that can be made to fail
questions.stem: A researcher proposes a hypothesis that cannot be tested; what is the main scientific problem?

options.text: It is too simple to be interesting
It will be proven true immediately
It cannot be checked against evidence
It requires too much funding

questions.explanation: Untestable hypotheses cannot be checked against evidence; simplicity or cost misdiagnose.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A journal of trials and the correspondence it carried
questions.learningObjective: Explain journal of trials and correspondence

stimulus.body: A journal records experimental trials and includes letters between investigators. The trials and correspondence together show how findings were tested and debated.

questions.stem: What does the journal with correspondence best show?

options.text: Only the final conclusions
That correspondence was private and irrelevant
That experiments were never repeated
How findings were tested and debated among investigators

questions.explanation: Trials plus correspondence show testing and debate; final-conclusions ignores process.

questions.topic: A society composed of judges rather than of specialists
questions.stem: A scientific society is composed of judges rather than specialists; what follows?

options.text: The society evaluates claims by general criteria rather than deep expertise
Judgments are always expert and technical
Specialists are banned from membership
No experiments are ever conducted

questions.explanation: Judges apply general criteria, not deep expertise; expert-judgment confuses roles.

questions.topic: Credit given to the man who worked the instrument
questions.stem: Credit is given to the man who worked the instrument; why might that be contested?

options.text: Because the instrument worker always deserves sole credit
Because instruments never produce real data
Because the designer or theorist may also deserve recognition
Because credit is irrelevant to science

questions.explanation: Instrument workers deserve credit but designers may too; sole-credit forecloses debate.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: The claim that air has weight, tested on a pump

stimulus.body: An experiment removes air from a sealed vessel on a balance. The vessel becomes lighter. The trial is repeated with controls.

questions.stem: What does the pump experiment test?

options.text: That air has no weight at all
That the balance is broken
That water is heavier than air
That air has weight, shown by the loss on removal

questions.explanation: Removal causing weight loss shows air has weight; no-weight reverses the finding.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A motto read as a statement of method

stimulus.body: A motto declares that we must begin from what can be doubted. It is read as a methodological rule rather than a conclusion.

questions.stem: How should the motto be read?

options.text: As a rule for starting inquiry by doubting
As a final proof of all knowledge
As a rejection of all science
As a religious creed

questions.explanation: The motto is a methodological rule to start by doubting; proof confuses method with conclusion.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: An explanation that outruns the trial that supports it
questions.stem: An explanation claims more than the trial supports; how should it be judged?

options.text: It should be accepted because it is elegant
It should be rejected as worthless
It overreaches and needs further testing
It proves the trial unnecessary

questions.explanation: Overreaching explanations need further testing; elegance or rejection extremes misjudge.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Beginning from nothing as a test for certainty
questions.stem: Why begin inquiry from nothing as a test for certainty?

options.text: To prove that nothing exists
To assert all knowledge is false
To avoid all experiments
To strip away assumptions and test what remains certain

questions.explanation: Beginning from nothing strips assumptions to test certainty; proving nothing exists confuses doubt with denial.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: A cut passage and what its author declined to say

stimulus.body: A passage is cut from a published work. The author declines to state why. Readers infer caution about a controversial claim.

questions.stem: What does the cut passage and reticence suggest?

options.text: The author was cautious about a controversial claim
The author forgot to include it
The author rejected the claim entirely
The passage was never written

questions.explanation: Reticence suggests caution about controversy; forgetting assumes accident.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Two procedures offered for the same failing

stimulus.body: Two procedures are offered for the same failing. One relies on observation, the other on authority. Results differ.

questions.stem: How should the two procedures be compared?

options.text: The authority-based procedure is always right
Both procedures are identical
The observation-based procedure should be tested against evidence
Neither procedure matters

questions.explanation: Observation-based procedure should be tested; authority-privilege misreads the comparison.

questions.topic: The year a manuscript plan could not be printed as it stood
questions.stem: A manuscript plan could not be printed as it stood in a given year; why?
